subject: Biology
title: Plants and Seasonal Change
description: A fast breakdown of Plants and Seasonal Change for builders.

hook.text: Plants track the seasons by measuring day length—a process called photoperiodism.

buildup.text: Short-day plants like chrysanthemums flower when nights grow long. Long-day plants flower in summer.

discovery.text: A pigment called phytochrome detects the ratio of red to far-red light, signaling day length.

twist.text: Deciduous trees drop their leaves to survive winter—frozen water in leaves would kill the cells.

climax.text: Climate change is shifting bloom times, sometimes causing plants and pollinators to fall out of sync.

punchline.text: Plants read the calendar with light, not dates.

quiz.question: How do plants measure day length?

details.summary: Plants detect seasonal changes through day length using photoreceptor proteins called phytochromes and cryptochromes. These signals trigger flowering, dormancy, leaf drop, and cold hardening, ensuring that critical events like reproduction occur at the optimal time of year.
details.whyItMatters: Climate change is disrupting seasonal timing for plants, causing mismatches with pollinators, premature bud break that risks frost damage, and altered growing seasons that affect both agriculture and natural ecosystems worldwide.
takeaways: Phytochromes detect changes in day length to trigger seasonal responses
Short-day plants flower when nights exceed a critical length in autumn
Cold hardening prepares plant cells for freezing by accumulating antifreeze proteins

faq.question: How do plants know what season it is?
faq.answer: Plants measure night length using phytochrome proteins that exist in two interconvertible forms depending on light exposure. Long nights signal autumn, triggering dormancy and leaf drop. Short nights signal summer, promoting growth. This photoperiodic sensing is remarkably precise.

faq.question: How is climate change affecting plant seasonal timing?
faq.answer: Warmer springs cause earlier bud break and flowering, sometimes weeks ahead of pollinators. Warm autumns delay dormancy, leaving plants vulnerable to sudden freezes. These phenological shifts disrupt ecological relationships and threaten crop yields.
